title: The condensed ring $\underline{\overline{\mathbf Q}}_\ell$
statement:
Let $\ell$ be a prime and $\Qlb$ an algebraic closure of $\mathbf Q_\ell$, with the
topology of the absolute value extending that of $\mathbf Q_\ell$. A *finite
subextension* is an intermediate field $\mathbf Q_\ell\subseteq E\subseteq\Qlb$ with
$[E:\mathbf Q_\ell]<\infty$. The finite subextensions, ordered by inclusion, form a
directed poset: the compositum of two of them is again one.

The condensed ring $\underline{\Qlb}$ on the pro-étale site of a point
$*_{\mathrm{proét}}$ ([sk-def-sfb-condensed-ring]) is defined by its sections

$$
\underline{\Qlb}(S):=\{a\in C(S,\Qlb)\mid a(S)\subseteq E\ \text{for some finite
subextension }E\},
$$

with restriction by precomposition and pointwise ring operations. In other words, it is
the subpresheaf of $C(-,\Qlb)$ of continuous maps with values in a finite subextension.
This is a sheaf of commutative rings, and it needs no sheafification. Its underlying
abelian sheaf is a commutative ring object of $\Sh(*_{\mathrm{proét}},\Ab)$
([sk-def-sfb-ring-object]).

proof.text: Finite subextensions and the ambient ring. By [det-def-sfb-qlbar-condensed-subextensions], the compositum of finitely many finite subextensions is finite and contains each of them. The base field $\mathbf Q_\ell$ is itself a finite subextension, so the inclusion poset is nonempty, and the two-field case gives directedness. Apply [def-sfb-continuous-map-condensed-ring] to the topological field $\Qlb$: $F(S)=C(S,\Qlb)$, with precomposition and pointwise operations, is a sheaf of commutative rings on the site of profinite sets.

source.place: Subring: finite compositum and ambient continuous-map ring

proof.text: Subring and restrictions. Put $G(S)=\{a\in F(S)\mid a(S)\subseteq E\text{ for some finite subextension }E\}$. If $a(S)\subseteq E$ and $b(S)\subseteq E'$, their sums, negatives and products lie in the finite compositum $EE'$ by [det-def-sfb-qlbar-condensed-subextensions]. These operations already belong to $F(S)$ by [def-sfb-continuous-map-condensed-ring]. The constant functions $0,1$, and all constants in $\mathbf Q_\ell$, satisfy the condition with $E=\mathbf Q_\ell$. Thus $G(S)$ is a commutative subring. For $u:S'\to S$, $(a\circ u)(S')\subseteq a(S)\subseteq E$, so precomposition restricts to a ring homomorphism $G(S)\to G(S')$. Identity and composite restrictions agree because composition of functions does; this defines exactly the presheaf in the statement.

Sheaf gluing without sheafification. Let $R$ be any covering sieve on a profinite set $S$ and let $(b_u)$ be a matching family with $b_u\in G(T)$ for every $u:T\to S$ in $R$. Under $G\subseteq F$, it is a matching family in the sheaf $F$ of [def-sfb-continuous-map-condensed-ring], so it has a unique glue $a\in F(S)$. By [sk-def-sfb-condensed-ring], $R$ contains a finite family $\pi_i:S_i\to S$ whose images jointly cover $S$. For each $i$, choose a finite subextension $E_i$ containing the image of $b_{\pi_i}=a\circ\pi_i$. Let $E$ be their finite compositum, using [det-def-sfb-qlbar-condensed-subextensions]. For every $s\in S$, choose $i$ and $t\in S_i$ with $\pi_i(t)=s$; then $a(s)=b_{\pi_i}(t)\in E_i\subseteq E$. Consequently $a\in G(S)$. Its restrictions along all of $R$ equal $b_u$, since they do in $F$, and any two glues in $G$ agree by uniqueness in $F$. When the chosen family is empty, joint surjectivity forces $S=\varnothing$ and the unique empty function satisfies the image condition with $E=\mathbf Q_\ell$. Thus the presheaf just constructed itself satisfies the sheaf condition. Because its operations are the pointwise ring operations and its restrictions are ring homomorphisms, these same unique glues make it a sheaf of commutative rings.

source.place: Sheaf: covering-sieve descent by a finite jointly surjective family

proof.text: Underlying ring object. Apply clause 3 of [sk-def-sfb-ring-object] to the sheaf of rings $G$ just constructed, on the site $*_{\mathrm{proét}}$. Its underlying abelian sheaf is a ring object of $\Sh(*_{\mathrm{proét}},\Ab)$, commutative because every section ring $G(S)$ is commutative. This is the asserted condensed ring and ring object, with the stated sections, restrictions and operations.
